title: I Used an AI Agent to Fix My Blog. Here's What It Found.
summary: A single unclosed tag took down every page on this site. I used an AI agent to find it — here's the honest account of what it caught, and what I had to decide myself.
content:
Last week someone told me my blog was showing a white screen. Not slow, not broken in one corner — blank. Every page. Every route. Just white.

Before I get into it, I should be straight about how this got done. I didn't debug this by hand. I used OpenHands, an open-source AI coding agent, and I directed it. I decided what to look at, what to fix, and what to ship. It did the reading, the searching, and the typing. That distinction matters to me, and I'll come back to it.

My first instinct was to open the live site and poke at it. My second instinct was better: read the code instead. So I told the agent to work from the local source and never pull the live copy down. That turned out to be the right call, because the answer was never on the screen. It was in the build.

One Character

The site is a React app. It builds into a single JavaScript bundle, and the whole thing is one page that swaps routes in the browser. That architecture is convenient right up until it isn't.

What the agent found was an unclosed tag. A single <article> in a page I'd added a few days earlier, opened and never closed. That's it. That's the whole bug.

But here's why one character erased an entire website: when a file has a syntax error, the bundler can't transform it. And if the bundler can't transform the file your app starts from, it doesn't ship a slightly broken bundle — it ships no bundle at all. The HTML loads, the stylesheet loads, the empty <div id="root"> sits there waiting for JavaScript that never arrives, and you get a white page. Every route. Because every route depends on the same one file.

The agent closed the tag and the site came back. That part took minutes.

The Part That Bothered Me

What bothered me wasn't the typo. It was that a typo could take the whole thing down silently.

Nothing in the project ran the build before the site shipped. No test, no check, no gate. So the question I actually sat with was uncomfortable: if one missing character can produce a blank website, and nothing is watching, then how many other missing characters are sitting in the code right now?

So I told the agent to keep reading.

What Else Was Wrong

The deeper it looked, the more the white screen stopped looking like bad luck and started looking like a warning.

Two CSS variables were being used but never defined. A folder of images had been moved without updating the paths that pointed at them, so dozens of images across the site were quietly 404-ing. One path was missing its leading slash, which meant it worked from the home page and broke everywhere else — the kind of bug that hides until someone shares a link. There was a dependency installed that nothing imported, and another that belonged in development sitting in production. Each of these was small. Together they told a story about a project that had grown faster than its guardrails.

None of that came from me staring at a screen. It came from an agent that could read the whole codebase faster than I could read one file, plus a browser tool that loaded every page and reported what actually rendered. That's the honest version. I used tools to find things I would have missed.

"Is This Build Ingenious?"

Someone asked me that, half joking. Is the build behind this site actually clever?

Honest answer: parts of it are, genuinely. The backend lives inside the build tool itself, which is unusual and a little unhinged but works. The login system uses real password hashing, signed sessions, and rate limiting — far more care than a personal blog strictly needs. And there's a hidden terminal game wired into it with its own progression and lore, which exists because I wanted it to.

I actually put that question to the agent, expecting it to be agreeable. It wasn't. It told me the clever parts were real, but that "ingenious" was the wrong word, because one stray character could still take the entire site down with nothing to catch it. That was a more useful answer than a compliment would have been.

Ingenious engineering is mostly about what can't go wrong, not what can go right. This build could go completely dark from one character. That's not a cleverness problem. It's a missing safety net problem, and safety nets are unglamorous by design.

Building the Net

So we stopped polishing and started defending.

The first change was the most important one: the site can no longer show a blank page. There's now a small script that runs before anything else loads, and if the app fails to start, it shows a real message with a reload button instead of nothing. If a page crashes while rendering, a boundary catches it and shows the same panel. Either way, a visitor sees an explanation, not a void.

The styling for that panel is deliberately inlined instead of living in the stylesheet, because if the bundle fails to load then the stylesheet never loads either. A fallback that depends on the thing that just broke isn't a fallback.

The second change was the net that should have existed all along: an automated check that loads the real built site in a real browser and confirms each page actually renders text. If a page is blank, the check fails. It even has a test for this exact incident — it deliberately blocks the JavaScript bundle and asserts that the fallback appears instead of a white screen.

Then we wired it into the pipeline so it runs before anything ships.

And to prove the net actually catches things, we broke the site on purpose. We added a line that throws an error on the home page, built it, and ran the check. It failed, and it named the page. Before, that same break would have been a white screen and a shrug. After, it's a red mark and a page name.

Cleanup as a Habit

The last pass was the boring one, and honestly the one I'm proudest of. Fixed the undefined styles. Repaired every broken image path. Removed the dependency nobody used — which turned out to drag eighty-six other packages along with it. Moved the misplaced one where it belonged. Cleared every warning until the linter ran completely clean, which meant it could finally be trusted to gate a release.

None of that is exciting. All of it is the difference between a project that feels solid and one that just looks solid.

What I'd Tell Anyone Else

Two things.

The first is about tools. I used an AI agent and a browser automation tool to fix my own website, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. But using a tool isn't the same as understanding the problem. I had to decide that the live site wasn't the place to look, that "the site is blank" was a build problem and not a hosting problem, and that a fix wasn't finished until something could prove it worked. The agent was fast and thorough. It was not in charge.

The second is about what the site actually needed. I started this thinking it needed to be more impressive. It didn't. It needed to be harder to break.

The site looks exactly the same as it did before any of this. Same pages, same writing, same design. But underneath, a page can't vanish anymore without something shouting about it first. That's not a feature anyone will notice. It's the reason the features I do have will keep working.

If you're building something and it feels fragile, the fix is usually not more cleverness. It's a net — one check, one fallback, one small thing that refuses to let a failure pass quietly. Start there. It's less fun than the feature. It's also what makes the feature worth having.
